name: FCC
title: How to Spot FCC Imposters
text:
Consumer Alert
Callers falsely claim that a consumer's phone number is under investigation for criminal activity. It's a scam!
Read the consumer alert [PDF]
The FCC has joined with partners across the country to shine a light on government and business imposter scams, which often target older Americans.
In these scams, bad actors pretending to be government agencies or well-known companies contact you by phone or text message and try to pressure you into handing over money, personal information, or access to your accounts.
Read the blog post
Help protect your community by spreading the word and joining the Elder Justice Coordinating Council’s “Never, Ever” campaign. Report incidents to the Federal Trade Commission.
Consumer Guide: Robocalls, Spoofing, Call Blocking
FCC Scam Glossary
Government imposter scams are one of the top reported scam categories every year. Fraudsters impersonate a government agency or official and claim that immediate payment is needed or that personal information must be verified in order to resolve a problem. Victims don't just lose money, they may also find that their identity is being used to commit fraud.
Savvy scammers have used the names of actual FCC employees. This makes the call seem more convincing.
Government imposters may also say they are from a business or bank and then say they need to transfer you to a government agent who will help you move your money into a “government account” for “safekeeping.”
It’s a lie.
If you think you've been contacted by phone, text, or email by an FCC or government imposter, do NOT respond.
If the contact is by phone, hang up immediately.
The FCC will never ask you for:
Payment of any kind over the phone — especially cash apps, crypto currency, gift cards, or store credit
Social Security number
driver's license number
bank account information
security information (PINs and Passwords) for any accounts, including banks, credit cards, social media accounts, your mobile devices (phones, laptops, tablets) or apps
The FCC will also never call or text you and threaten to take action if you don’t give us money or personal information.
We do not accept payment in cash, cash apps, crypto currency, store credit accounts, or gift cards. If someone claiming to be from the FCC asks for such a payment, it's a red flag.
Talk to someone you trust if you’re worried about a problem with your account or identity — especially if the stranger says they’re from the government or the situation is serious or involves a crime.
If the call or text you received includes a threat of violence or harm to you or anyone else, immediately report it to local law enforcement.
File a Complaint With the FCC
Report FCC imposter scams using our online complaint form. When filing a complaint, please select the form "Phone" and the issue "Unwanted Calls/Texts." Please include as much information as possible about the incident, including date and time of contact, names and phone numbers, the call topic, and what the caller said or requested.
Once you file a complaint, you will receive an email from the FCC with a confirmation that your complaint has been received. There is no fee for filing an informal complaint.
